newsitem.title: CONGO: Congo budget sets 32.4 percent spending boost.
newsitem.headline: Congo budget sets 32.4 percent spending boost.

text.p: Parliament approved Congo's 1997 budget with spending up 32.4 percent at 493.9 billion CFA francs ($881 million), on the expectation of higher revenues.

The official Congo News Agency said the government expected total revenues of 442.75 billion CFA and would make up the budget shortfall of 51 billion CFA through borrowing from official and multilateral creditors.

International Monetary Fund officials said the budget appeared to have passed the last hurdle, the Senate or upper house, without amendments and its adoption is expected remove one problem in the Central African country's dealings with the IMF and its other creditors.
The Congo News Agency quoted the government as saying increased spending was justified by a projected rise in revenues, despite the persistence of deficits.
Congo expects higher revenues both from a rise in oil exports and from an improved economy overall, the agency said.

Oil exports received a big boost with the inauguration last June of Elf-Aquitaine's offshore Nkossa production, which is expected to push Congo's annual oil production to 13 million tonnes this year from nine million tonnes.
Parliament last week adopted a law for the introduction of Value Added Tax at the rate of 18 percent this year as part of measures to boost internal revenues.
The government said the leap in spending was necessitated by debt-servicing, the cost of organising presidential elections next July and the government's programme to fight poverty.

The approval by parliament of the 1997 budget was one of the conditions for continuing financial assistance laid down by the IMF in its November 1996 review of Congo's efforts to get its economic house in order.
Congo's other creditors, such as the so-called Paris Club of creditor nations, have all made their continuing assistance dependent on the country sticking to the IMF's programme.

Senators criticised the short notice at which the budget was brought before parliament. They called on the government to take action to remedy the deterioration of infrastructure and services throughout the country after concern was expressed by local authorities.
The administration has been functioning since the beginning of the year on part of a provisional budget after a decree was passed to that effect at the beginning of January.
